lawyer:
Rafique-ul-Huq with Md Mizanul Haque Chowdhury Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 

Md Rezaul Islam, Assistant Attorney-General ------ For Respondents.
parties:
Uricon Trading ------ Petitioner
vs. 
Commissioner of Customs and others ------  Respondents
full_judgment:
<u>Md Abdur Rashid J: In the above writ petitioners, assessment of duties and other charges on the basis of tariff value on the imported goods of the petitioner was challenged.</u>

2. Upon further applications on the behalf of the petitioner, on 1-8-06 in the above three Writ Petitions and on 3-7-06 in Writ Petition No. 108 of 1998 supplementary Rule Nisi was issued against constitutionality of SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95.

3. First two writ petitions arise out of assessment of customs duty and other charges on imported goods, namely, 'Caustic Soda' while in the latter two petitions, imported goods was Soda Ash'. As the petitioner is the same in all the writ petitions and the issues involved are also common, we heard the writ petitions together and now, dispose of them by this order.

4. The petitioner is an importer. In Writ Petition No. 107 of 1998, he on 18-12-97 opened a letter of credit for import of Caustic Soda. After arrival of the goods at Chittagong two bills of entry being No. C-32211 and C-32215 were submitted on 8-1-98 for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value at the rate of US$ 190 per metric ton.

5. Some date the concerned customs authority ordered for assessment for the imported goods on the basis of tariff value at the rate of US$ 375 per metric ton by way of adjustment at the rate of 1.9348% on the basis of tariff value. In the supplementary affidavit, in support of C&F value, the petitioner annexed number of documents under 'H' series to show CRF certified value of said 'Caustic Soda', which never exceeded US$ 260 per metric ton in the immediate past.

6. It is also stated that the National Board of Revenue by a circular dated 12-11-97 recorded price of Caustic Soda of origin of China classified under HS Code No. 2815.11.00 at the rate of US$ 260 per metric ton (Annexure-1) and by further notification dated 4-6-98 the Finance Ministry further clarified that such value would override the tariff value.

7. In Writ Petition No. 1443 of 1998, letter of credit was established on 16-4-98 for import of Caustic Soda and after arrival of the goods at Chittagong two bills of entry being C-60496 and C-60499 were submitted on 26-5-98 for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value at the rate of US $ 189 per metric ton.

8. The concerned Customs Authority however ordered to impose tariff value at the rate of US$ 375 per metric ton by way of adjustment at the rate of 1.9451. In the application for supplementary rule the petitioner also annexed same documents as in the earlier supplementary affidavit as Annexure-H series and T and I(1) in support of C&F values.

9. In the Writ Petition No. 108 of 1998, letter of credit was established on 18-12-97 for import of Soda Ash and after arrival of the goods, three bills of entry were submitted on 8-1-98 for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value at the rate of US$ 131 per metric ton but the concerned customs authority imposed tariff value at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton by way of adjustment at the rate of 1.6463 by SRO notification No. 26 dated 11-10-97.

10. In the application for supplementary rule, the petitioner annexed amongst other decision of the valuation committee dated 11-10-99, which after consideration of various prices found US$ 138 per metric ton highest recorded value of such Soda Ash at the contemporary period would be more reasonable (Annexure-1) and CRF certificate issued by an approved PSI agent certifying the price of 'Soda Ashes' never exceeded US$ 160 per metric ton within last decade and those values were accepted by the customs authority as Annexure-J, K, and L series. The petitioner also annexed copy of a unreported judgment dated 8-8-05 passed in Writ Petition No. 6687 of 1997 by this Division, which fixed US$ 160 per metric ton as price of 'Soda Ash' during the period.

11. In Writ Petition No. 1349 of 1998, letter of credit was established 16-4-98 for import of Soda Ash and after arrival of said goods six bills of entry were on 21-5-98 submitted for release of the goods at the rate of C&F value of US$ 128 per metric ton. But the concerned customs authority ordered for assessment at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton on the basis of tariff value by notification No. 30 dated 1-12-97 by way of adjustment at the rate of adjustment 01.6849. In the application for supplementary rule, the petitioner annexed aforesaid documents annexed to writ petition No. 108 in support of the price of Soda Ash as Annexure-I series, K and L series. The petitioner also annexed aforesaid judgment dated 8-8-05 passed in Writ Petition No. 6687 of 1997.

12. Mr. Rafique-ul-Haq, the learned senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner took us through the record and several SROs and submitted that SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-98 was already declared to be without any lawful authority and of no legal effect by a Division Bench of this Division in Writ Petition No. 2017 of 1997 dated 26-11-06 with the result that the assessment of customs duty and other charges on the imported goods namely Caustic Soda and Soda Ash by the customs authority at the rate of tariff value, which was far higher than that of recorded CRF value at the relevant time was unauthorized and arbitrary.

13. He submitted that the petitioner produced numbers of documents in support of the C&F value which was backed even by a decision of the customs authority and also a decision of this Division but the customs authority loaded tariff value which was higher than the recorded value and beyond international market price and, as such, the assessment was arbitrary and illegal.

14. In support, he cited aforesaid judgments passed in Writ Petition Na. 2017 of 1997 (Caustic Soda) and Writ Petition No. 6687 of 1997 (Soda Ash) and Salim vs Commissioner of Customs 56 DLR 228 of which one of us is the author.

15. On behalf of the customs authority no affidavit-in-opposition could be filed. Mr. Md Rezaul Islam, learned Assistant Attorney-General however, tried to defend the assessment orders on the basis of tariff value, which would prevail C&F value.

16. Only issue, in the facts and circumstances of the cases, that is facing as is whether or not the decision of the customs authority assessing the value of the imported goods on the basis of tariff value as per relevant notification was well founded and lawful.

17. In the first two writ petitions as stated hereinbefore imported goods were Caustic Soda while in the last two ones Soda Ash. After arrival of the goods, bills of entry were submitted on behalf of the petitioner for release of the goods on the basis of C&F value. In support of said value, number of documents was produced including decision of the customs authority, the government and this Division on the price of the imported goods at the relevant period.

18. In the first two writ petitioners we find that the National Board of Revenue on 12-11-97 circulated a direction to the effect that the price of Caustic Soda of origin of China was recorded at the rate of US$ 260 per metric ton and to be classified under HS Code No. 2815.11.00, (Annexure-I). It further directed that if the said value was in force on 30-6-98 then said goods ought to be assessed upon such value. If tariff value was fixed upon the goods and higher than the recorded value, then the duty would to be assessed on tariff value. When recorded value was higher than the tariff value, then duty would be assessed on such recorded value.

19. The Finance Ministry however, by its notification SRO No. 50 dated 4-6-98 notified that the tariff value would not apply in case of goods recorded in the schedule, (Annexure-1(1). The legal effect of two Annexure-I and I(1) was clearly intended to override the tariff value as notified by notification No. 33 dated 30-12-97 vis-a-vis recorded value. It also appears from the copies of PSI certificates for the period from 10-5-02 to 3-11-05 (Annexure-H series) submitted by the petitioner in support of its value the price of Caustic Soda never crossed US$ 257 per metric ton.

20. In view of such materials, we are unable to accept the valuation of Caustic Soda at the rate of tariff value at US$ 375 per metric ton as nearest ascertainable international market price. Consequently, the valuation of the customs authority of Caustic Soda must be held to be inflated and arbitrary.

21. In respect of valuation of imported Soda Ash, we find in the unreported case of Ms. Kemal Trading Co Ltd, writ petition No. 6677 of 1997 dated 8-8-05 that the value of Soda Ash at the time of submission of bills of entry for clearance of Soda Ash on 15-10-97 was considered. In the case, the customs authority also valued Soda Ash on the basis of tariff value at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton. A Division Bench of this Division found that the fixation of tariff value at the rate of US$ 220 per metric ton was inflated and that there was no justification in the increase of tariff value from US$ 160 to 220 and accordingly, held that the importer was entitled to get imported consignment assessed at the rate of tariff value of US$ 160. We are told that the decision has not been challenged. If so, we do not find any reason to take a view different from said decision on the valuation of Soda Ash.

22. Originally section 25 of the Customs Act amongst other provided that value of imported goods liable to customs duty should be the actual price that is the price actually paid or payable, or the nearest ascertainable equivalent of such price. Sub-section (2) of said section also provided for determination of the price in respect of imported goods in accordance with the rules that may be made in this behalf. In the absence of the rules, sometime, the government fixed tariff value for the purpose of assessment. Then, section 25A was introduced.

<u>23. Original scheme of section 25 has undergone change by amendment number of times. But the intention remained the same that the imported goods should be assessed on the actual price or nearest equivalent of the international market price. The device for determination of the value was discovered and older ones updated time to time primarily to prevent the unscrupulous importers from evading and/or cheating the government revenue.</u>

24. In the case of Md Salim, one of us was the author the view taken on determination of the value of imported goods for assessment on the basis of invoice value vis-a-vis tariff value was as follows:

“It is clear from the above provision that customs duty is to be levied on the actual price or the nearest equivalent of such price the imported goods would fetch on a sale in the international market between a buyer and seller independent of each other. Sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Customs Act no doubt, empowers the Government to fix by notification in the official gazette tariff value for the goods imported or exported for the purpose of levying customs duty. But such price is not conclusive and an importer or exporter, as the case may be, is always entitled to prove the actual price of such goods.

In the case before us, the importer produced duly endorsed and attested invoices quoting the price of the imported goods. In the absence of any document whatsoever to the contrary, such invoice value cannot be ignored."

25. We are told that the decision was not challenged. Tariff value as notified by the Government time to time cannot be said to be infallible. The importer is always entitled to have his goods assessed on the basis of the price he paid or ascertainable equivalent of such price in the international market under sub-section (1) if section 25 and prove such price at the time of assessment.

26. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq strenuously challenged the constitutionality of SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95. He wanted to impress upon us saying that the value of Caustic Soda or Soda Ash at the relevant time of import could not be higher than the CRF certified value as well. He also submitted that the government most illegally took away Caustic Soda and Soda Ash from the schedule of SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. He submitted that in view of section 25A of the Customs Act and said SRO No.316, the petitioner had vested right to have his imported goods assessed not higher than the CRF certified value even when he imported the goods after the exclusion of said goods by SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95. In support, he relied upon the unreported decision dated 26-11-06 of a Division Bench of this Division in the case of Mohammad Zakir vs the Commissioner of Customs in Writ Petition No.2017, wherein said SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 was declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect.

27. Section 25A of the Customs Act appears to be first introduced by the Finance Act, 1994 with effect from 1st day of July, 1994. Said section empowers the Government by notification in the official gazette of declare the quality, quantity, price, description and customs classification of any goods verified and certified in the prescribed manner by an approved pre-shipment agency shall be accepted as the basis for assessment notwithstanding any other provisions in the Customs Act. Result ensued that such certified value would override all other value including the tariff value.

28. The Government also issued SRO No.316 dated 3-11-94 to carry out the purpose of said section 25A. It appears certain goods were time to time taken out of the purview of said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 for PSI certification.

29. In the case of the Commissioner of Customs vs Monhar Ali, the Appellate Division noticed that by SRO No.244 dated 31-12-96 12 certain goods were taken out of said SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94 of the scheme of CRF certification by a pre-shipment agency. The importer in the case conscious of such change imported various goods, which were not included in said SRO No.244, and the goods arrived with certification by approved PSI agency. Long after the opening of the letter of credits, SRO No. 113 dated 11-5-97 was issued, which fixed tariff value on the goods, described in schedule-1 including those of the petitioner. The Appellate Division affirmed the decision of this Division that the importer had vested right to have his goods assessed on the value that was prevalent at the time of opening of the letter of credit.

<u>30. In the case in our hands, SRO No. 215 was issued on 12-12-95 taking Caustic Soda and Soda Ash out of the purview of SRO No. 316 dated 3-11-94. Knowing fully well of such change, the importer opened letter of credit on 18-12-97; 16-4-98; 18-12-97 and 16-4-98 respectively in the aforesaid writ petitions.</u>

<u>31. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq challenged SRO No. 215 taking out of the vested rights of the importer on two counts, first, the authority of the Government in issuing such notification and then, constitutionality of the notification. His submissions on the authority of the Government and vested right of the importer did not appeal us at all. But in view of the decision of another Division Bench in above case of Mohammad Zakir and the merit of the case on the valuation, we did not find any need to dwell such upon the question of constitutionality of SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95.</u>

32. Immediate after dictation of this judgment, an unreported decision dated 6-8-05 of the Appellate Division in the case of Nasiruddin Ahmed vs. the Commissioner of Customs in Civil Appeal No. 102 of 1998 came to our notice. In the case, this Division found SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 constitutional in the following terms,

"So, the authority which issued the SRO (316) dated 3-11-94 also amended the aforesaid SRO vide issuing another SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 under section 25A of the said Act. As such we do not find any reason as to why this amended Notification dated 12-12-95 should be called ultra-vires section 25A of the Customs Act or the previous SRO No.316 dated 3-11-94. Since the self-same authority, which issued the SRO No.316 dated 316, had also issued this amended SRO on 12-12-95. We are of the view that there is no illegality on the part of the authority to issue the above amended SRO does not in any way infringe the provision of section 25A of the Customs Act or the previous SRO dated 3-11-94."

33. In disposing of the appeal, the Appellate Division approved the above view of this Division regarding SRO No. 215 dated 12-12-95 in the above case and other writ petitions. The Appellate Division however, dismissed the appeal of the importer holding that the assessment of duties on the basis of Yellow Book value for the imported reconditioned cars and vehicles from abroad could not be said to be illegal and without jurisdiction.

<u>34. Earlier decision of this Division in WP No.201 of 1996 approved by the Appellate Division declaring the SRO No.215 dated 12-12-95 constitutional was not brought to the notice of the Division Bench neither in the case of Md Zakir nor to us. In view of endorsement by the Appellate Division to the earlier decision in Nasiruddin Ahmed, decision of this Division in Md Zakir was not the correct statement of law. Now, none else but the Bar should take the responsibility for this Division to be trapped in to find the wrong end of law in the latter case of Md Zakir. We could not help but to take the pain to make the record straight in the light of the decision of the Appellate Division on the constitutionality of SRO No.215 dated 12-12-95.</u>

<u>35. For the aforesaid reasons, there is however, no escape from the conclusion that the assessments on the basis of the tariff value by the customs authority of duty and other charges of the imported goods, namely, Caustic Soda and Soda Ash must be held to be arbitrary and cannot be sustained in law.</u>

<u>36. In the result, all the writ petitions are made absolute without however any order as to cost. Assessment made of Caustic Soda and Soda Ash on the basis of tariff value are hereby declared to have been made without any lawful authority and as such, of no legal effect.</u>

37. The concerned customs authority is hereby directed to assess said imported goods in the light of our above observations and as per the valuation of imported goods rule, 1997 and shall refund the Bank Guarantee received, after receipt of the balance, due if any, in cash on final assessment within a period of thirty days of receipt of this order, positively.

Communicate at once.

End.
